opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest difference is access. With a neural network, we can see everything. Every activation, every weight, every intermediate computation is just sitting there as numbers. We can record all of it, perfectly, for every input. Neuroscientists would kill for that. With a human brain, you're looking through these very coarse windows: fMRI gives you blood flow averaged over millions of neurons and a couple of seconds, EEG gives you electrical signals smeared across the scalp, and the really precise recordings, like single-neuron electrodes, you can only do in a handful of cells, usually in animals or in patients who are already undergoing surgery.

The second big difference is intervention. In a model, I can go in and say, "What happens if I set this neuron to zero?" or "What if I take the activation from one input and patch it into another?" and rerun it a million times, at no cost and with no ethical concerns. That lets you do real causal experiments, not just correlational ones. In neuroscience, causal interventions exist, like lesion studies, optogenetics, and stimulation, but they're expensive, slow, and very constrained.

That said, I don't want to oversell it, because having perfect access doesn't mean you understand what you're looking at. That's the humbling part of interpretability. We have all the data, and we still often can't explain why a model does what it does. Individual neurons tend to be polysemantic, responding to lots of unrelated things, and the meaningful concepts are spread across many dimensions. So in a sense we've hit some of the same conceptual problems neuroscience has: What's the right unit of analysis? Is it a neuron, a direction in activation space, a circuit? What does it even mean to "explain" a computation?

So I'd say the AI case is much easier experimentally and just as hard conceptually. And I think that's actually exciting, because models can serve as a kind of testbed. If we can't develop methods that work when we have perfect access, that's a pretty strong signal those methods won't work on brains either. And if we do find methods that work, maybe some of those ideas can flow back into neuroscience.

r001.rationale: The response says precise recordings from human brains are limited to a handful of cells, usually during surgery, and describes neuroscience interventions as constrained. It does not state that inserting an electrode merely to check activity would be unjustified even with complete understanding of the brain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that it's a difference in access more than a difference in kind, and the access gap is enormous.

With a neural network, we have perfect observability. I can read every single activation, every weight, at every layer, for every token. I can rerun exactly the same input a thousand times and get exactly the same internal state. And crucially, I can intervene. I can reach in, add a vector to the residual stream, zero out a component, swap an activation from one run into another, and see precisely what changes in the output. That causal control is the thing neuroscientists would give anything for.

With a human brain, you have none of that. fMRI gives you a blurry average of blood flow over seconds, when the computation happens in milliseconds. Single-cell recordings give you beautiful resolution but for a few hundred neurons out of eighty-some billion. You can't rerun the same brain on the same stimulus with the same state. And interventions are either crude, like lesions or stimulation, or ethically off the table. Neuroscience has basically been doing interpretability with one hand tied behind its back for a century.

So in principle we're in a much better position. But what's humbling is that even with that perfect access, we still mostly don't understand what these models are doing. You can see every number and still not know what the computation means. That tells you the hard part was never the measurement. The hard part is finding the right level of description, the right units of analysis. Is it individual neurons? Directions in activation space? Circuits? Features that are smeared across many neurons in superposition? We're still arguing about that, and neuroscience has been arguing about the equivalent question for a long time.

The other big difference is that we built these systems, but not in a way that helps. We wrote the training process, not the learned algorithm. So we're in this strange position of being the creator and still having to do reverse engineering, almost like archaeology on something we made last week.

What I find exciting is the traffic going both ways. Techniques like causal mediation and representational similarity came from cognitive science and neuroscience, and now people in interpretability are developing methods, like sparse autoencoders or activation patching, that neuroscientists are starting to look at as hypotheses for how to think about biological representations. Models are a kind of model organism. They're a place where you can test whether your theories of understanding a neural system actually work, because there, at least, the ground truth is fully available if you're clever enough to find it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts model access with limited and ethically constrained brain measurements, but it does not state that complete understanding of the brain would not justify inserting an electrode merely to check its activity.

astra-6.text:
The biggest difference is access. With an AI model, you can, in principle, record every internal activation and inspect every weight. You can also intervene: change an activation, remove a component, run the same input again, and see how the output changes. With a human brain, we don’t have that kind of comprehensive, precise access, and there are obvious ethical limits on what experiments we can do.

But access isn’t the same as understanding. Having all those numbers doesn’t automatically tell you, “This is where the model forms a belief,” or, “This is why it gave that answer.” You still have to figure out what the activity means and test whether your interpretation actually explains the behavior.

So AI gives us a much more accessible experimental system, but we still face a problem familiar from neuroscience: how do you turn a description of internal activity into an explanation of what the system is doing?

r001.rationale: The response mentions ethical limits on experiments involving human brains, but does not state that even complete understanding would not justify inserting an electrode merely to check activity.

sol-6.1.text:
The big difference is access. With an AI model, we can, in principle, record every internal activation, inspect the weights, and intervene on particular components. We can run the same input again after changing something and see how the output changes. With a human brain, our measurements and interventions are much more limited.

But access isn’t the same as understanding. Seeing all the numbers inside a model doesn’t automatically tell you what those numbers mean, or why it produced a particular answer. You still have to develop hypotheses and test them. So AI gives us a much more accessible experimental system, but we shouldn’t confuse having a complete record of its activity with having a complete explanation of its behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says measurements and interventions in the human brain are limited, but it does not state that even complete understanding would not justify inserting an electrode merely to check activity.
